content: The findings are entered into the tool as the health worker conducts the examination. All other signs are either normal or absent. The tool does not prompt any further assessments, tests, or laboratory investigations for Jacob. Upon completing the assessment, the tool suggests a classification of illness. It indicates that Jacob has pneumonia, no acute malnutrition, and no anemia. Additionally, the tool identifies that Jacob meets the criteria for prevention, screening, and other health interventions, and recommends that he receive vaccinations and vitamin A supplementation. The health worker is given the option to agree or disagree with each of the classifications proposed by the tool. The health worker agrees with all the proposed classifications. For each classification, the tool provides recommended treatments and management strategies. For pneumonia, the tool suggests treating Jacob with oral amoxicillin, specifying the appropriate dose, frequency, and duration of treatment based on his age, weight, and illness classification. The tool also reminds the health worker that Jacob should return to the clinic for follow-up in three days to monitor his pneumonia. Since Jacob has not received vitamin A, the tool reminds the health worker that he is eligible for vitamin A supplementation during this visit and prompts the health worker to administer any vaccinations for which Jacob is eligible. The tool prompts the health worker to assess Jacob for any feeding problems and provides reminders about counseling that should be given to Amira, Jacob’s caregiver, to ensure proper care at home. This includes advice on a safe remedy to soothe Jacob’s cough, feeding recommendations, instructions on administering the prescribed medication, and guidance on when to return to the clinic. The health worker counsels Amira on how to treat Jacob’s pneumonia, administer the antibiotic and throat remedy at home, and emphasizes the importance of bringing Jacob back in three days for a follow-up. The health worker also reviews with Amira the warning signs she should watch for and explains that if Jacob exhibits any of these signs, she should return to the clinic immediately. Finally, the health worker saves Jacob’s record in the digital tool. Aisha, a 23-year-old mother, brings her two-and-a-half-year-old son, Abbas, to a primary healthcare facility because he has been sick for the past few days. The health worker asks Aisha if this is Abbas’s first visit to the facility. Aisha explains that she had previously brought Abbas to the facility for a different problem when he was younger. The health worker inquires about the reason for today’s visit, and Aisha reports that Abbas has had a cough for a few days. The health worker searches for Abbas in the registered patients list using his name and date of birth and locates his profile, which already contains his basic demographic information and details about Aisha and Abbas’s father. The health worker selects Abbas’s profile and initiates a new consultation. The health worker begins by checking for any danger signs of severe illness in Abbas, as prompted by the tool. Since Abbas does not exhibit any danger signs, the consultation proceeds. The health worker measures Abbas’s temperature, weight, mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), and height, as prompted by the tool. The tool calculates Abbas’s weight-for-height and weight-for-age z-scores, both of which are normal (z-score = 0). The health worker is then prompted to check for symptoms of illness. Abbas has a cough, and when this is entered into the tool, it suggests an additional question about the duration of the cough. The health worker asks Aisha how long Abbas has been coughing, and based on her response, enters 4 days into the tool. All other symptoms are either absent or normal. The health worker then asks Aisha for Abbas’s health record to review his history of HIV counseling and testing, vaccination status, and the last doses of vitamin A and deworming. Next, the health worker conducts a physical examination to look for signs of illness. The tool reminds the health worker to evaluate specific signs based on Abbas’s age and symptoms, including respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. The health worker observes that Abbas is wheezing and measures his oxygen saturation, which is 89%. When this information is entered into the tool, a pop-up highlights that Abbas’s oxygen saturation is critically low and reminds the health worker to ensure the measurement was performed correctly, administer oxygen if available, and complete the assessment quickly to avoid delaying referral. After entering all data and signs into the system, the tool suggests that Abbas has severe pneumonia with wheezing. Based on the health worker’s observations, they agree with this diagnosis. The tool recommends pre-referral treatment with intramuscular ampicillin and gentamicin, as well as a fast-acting bronchodilator. The health worker arranges for Abbas to be referred to a hospital and explains to Aisha that Abbas likely has severe pneumonia and requires further treatment at the hospital. The health worker asks Aisha if she has any questions or concerns and saves the information about Abbas’s visit in the tool. Radha brings her young infant, Savi, to the clinic for the first time since Savi was born. Radha is concerned because Savi’s skin appears yellow. The health worker registers Savi in the tool by entering her name, date of birth, sex, and other demographic information. Savi’s profile is saved in the tool, which will include information about her and her caregivers for future visits. The health worker then opens a new consultation for Savi and selects sick infant/child as the visit type due to Savi’s problem. The tool prompts the health worker to evaluate whether Savi has any signs of a life-threatening illness, based on her age. After recording in the tool that Savi has no signs of a life-threatening illness, the health worker collects basic measurements, including Savi’s weight and temperature. When Savi’s temperature is entered into the tool, it prompts the health worker to inform Radha that the temperature is normal for a baby of Savi’s age. However, when Savi’s weight is entered, the tool calculates her weight-for-age z-score and alerts the health worker that it is low. The health worker asks Radha about Savi’s problems, and Radha explains that she noticed Savi’s skin was yellow, which was different from her other babies when they were little. The tool prompts the health worker to ask about symptoms of possible illnesses or problems, including whether Savi has had convulsions, how she is feeding, whether she has diarrhea, and whether she is breastfed. Radha confirms that none of these symptoms are present and that Savi is breastfed. The health worker records this information in the tool. Next, the health worker assesses what health promotion and screening services Savi has recently received, including Radha’s HIV counseling and testing history and Savi’s vaccination history. The health worker reviews Savi’s child health card and confirms with Radha that she was tested for HIV during pregnancy and had a negative result. Savi received vaccinations at the hospital when she was born. This information is entered into the tool. The health worker conducts a physical examination of Savi, observing her breathing, ensuring there is no chest indrawing, counting her breaths per minute, and observing her movements. They examine her skin and umbilicus for signs of infection and assess the color of her skin. When the health worker enters into the tool that Savi has yellow skin, the tool prompts a question about when jaundice first appeared. Radha states that the yellow skin appeared yesterday, when Savi was three days old. The health worker records that the jaundice began after the first 24 hours of life. The health worker discusses Savi’s feeding practices with Radha to learn more about her breastfeeding habits and enters this information into the tool. They then observe Radha breastfeeding Savi to ensure there are no feeding problems. Finding no issues, the health worker records this in the tool. After completing the look, listen, and feel components of the consultation, the tool provides a list of proposed classifications for Savi: unlikely infection, jaundice, feeding problem or low weight-for-age, and unlikely HIV infection. The health worker reviews these classifications, considers their observations during the consultation, and agrees with them. The tool then provides a list of treatments and management options for each classification, including counseling on appropriate breastfeeding, keeping the baby warm, and caring for the baby at home. The health worker explains to Radha that Savi has jaundice but reassures her that it can be managed at home. They ask Radha to return with Savi the next day to check on the jaundice and in 14 days to monitor Savi’s weight. The health worker provides feeding recommendations, explains how to keep the baby warm at home, and reminds Radha of the signs that require immediate return to the clinic, such as yellow palms or soles. Finally, the health worker saves the consultation information in the tool.
